# Exercises

## Exercise 1: Arachnopobia and the Binomial Distribution

A Gallup Poll found that 7% of teenagers (ages 13 to 17) suffer from arachnophobia and are extremely afraid of spiders. At a summer camp there are 10 teenagers sleeping in each tent. Assume that these 10 teenagers are independent of each other. 

**a.** Let $X$ be the number of teenagers in a tent of 10 teenagers who suffer from arachnophobia. Precisely explain why $X$ follows a Binomial(n,p) distribution, and state what values $n$ and $p$ are.

# Mini-Lecture: Continuous Random Variables 



## Exercise 2: Practice with Continuous Random Variables 

Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the density function visualized below.

```{r fig.height=3, echo = F}
t <- seq(0, 3, length = 200)
p <- rep(0, 200)
p[t <= 2] <- 0.4
p[t > 2] <- -0.4 * t[t > 2] + 1.20

dd <- data.frame(t, p)
(gg <- ggplot(dd, aes(x = t, y = p)) + geom_area(fill = "gray", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Density", title = "Density of X"))
```

**a.** By eye, calculate $P(X \leq 1)$ (visualized below).

```{r fig.height=3, echo = F}
gg + geom_ribbon(data = subset(dd, t > 0 & t <= 1), aes(ymax = p),
                 ymin = 0, fill = "red", alpha = .75)
```

*******************************************************************************



*******************************************************************************


**b.** By eye, calcualte $P(X \leq 2)$.

```{r fig.height=3, echo = F}
gg + geom_ribbon(data = subset(dd, t > 0 & t <= 2), aes(ymax = p),
                 ymin = 0, fill = "red", alpha = .75)
```

*******************************************************************************



*******************************************************************************


**c.** By eye, calculate $P(2 \leq X \leq 3)$.

```{r fig.height=3, echo = F}
gg + geom_ribbon(data = subset(dd, t > 2 & t <= 3), aes(ymax = p),
                 ymin = 0, fill = "red", alpha = .75)
```

*******************************************************************************

## Exercise 3: Probabilities and Quantiles

For Exercise 1, we can use `pbinom()` to easily calculate probabilities like $P(X \leq k)$ when $X$ follows a *Binomial* distribution. We can use `R` to make similar calculations for continuous random variable distributions! 

Tomorrow, we'll learn about the *Normal* distribution (colloquially, bell-shaped curves). `R` follows similar naming conventions, so if $X$ follows a Normal distribution and we want to calculate a **cumulative probability** $P(X \leq q)$, we can use `pnorm(q, mu, sigma)`, where `mu` and `sigma` are distribution parameters representing the mean and standard deviation of $X$ (we'll learn more about this tomorrow). For now, we'll assume that `mu = 0` and `sigma = 1`, which are the default settings in `R` when we just call `pnorm(q)`. 

**a.** The chunk below visualizes a Normal random variable $X$ (with `mu = 0` and `sigma = 1`), and a vertical line representing $X = 1$.

```{r}
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(-4, 4)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, geom = "area", fill = "magenta4", alpha = 0.25) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, color = "magenta4", lwd = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1), color = "dodgerblue", lwd = 1, lty = 2) +
  labs(title = "", x = "X", y = "")
```

In a new chunk below, use `R` to calculate $P(X \leq 1)$, i.e. the area to the *left* of the blue dashed line. 

*******************************************************************************



*******************************************************************************


**b.** Below, play around with calculating probabilities for various points under the Normal distribution above. What happens when you use smaller versus larger values of `q` in `pnorm(q)`?

*******************************************************************************



*******************************************************************************



**c.** Soon in this class, we'll be very interested in calculating **quantiles** of distributions like this one. For example, we might want to find the 0.95 quantile, or the point $q$ where 95% of the area under the curve is to the left of $q$. Lucky for us, `R` has functions to help us do this for several distributions. For this normal distribution, `qnorm(p)` will return the **quantile** (on the x-axis) of a given **cumulative probability** $p$ (it will give us $q$ such that $P(X \leq q) = p$).

Use `qnorm()` to calculate the **0.85** quantile of our Normal distribution above. Does it make sense to you that this value is close to the blue dashed line above?
